_doc: Service life of a durable good: the years a stock of it serves before it is worn out or lost, so users hold it and buy only to keep it up (the economy reads a good with a service life as a durable; a good not listed is used up within the year). Keyed by the good ids of data/production. Estimates, confidence C or D; a wear model per good (use, material, maintenance) would derive them. Carts are not goods in the production data yet, so they have no entry; timber, cloth and other materials that are also consumed as inputs are left out until a held-stock model separates the two uses.

iron_tools_kg.source: FAO, 'Contribution of farm power to smallholder livelihoods in sub-Saharan Africa', Annex 3 Table 5 'Replacement rates (years) of tools and equipment by field site', fao.org/4/a0229e/a0229e0i.htm, opened: hoe replacement at ten sites in Ghana, Nigeria, Tanzania, Malawi and Zambia 1, 2, 2-4, 1-2, 3, 2, 1.5, 1, 2, 3 years; taking range midpoints the mean is 2.0 years (20 divided by 10). The main text (fao.org/docrep/pdf/011/aj334e/aj334e02.pdf, 'Replacement of Tools', opened) adds that hoes were replaced every year where blacksmiths use scrap steel and that with better steel 'the life of a hoe was calculated to be anything from two to 15 years'. Modern African smallholder hoes, not Roman or medieval ones: an analogue used as the nearest measured figure (was 4, no source). Axes and sickles in the same table last longer, so a mixed tool kit outlives the hoe; the hoe is the farm tool this good stands for.

wooden_tools_kg.source: LABELLED HEURISTIC, no source found for the working life of a wooden hoe, spade or rake before wear or breakage; taken as half an iron tool's (2 years, FAO hoe replacement above), since wood wears and splits faster than iron; searched in the Complaint 650 pass and again in the 670 pass and no timed wear study of wooden farm tools was found; retire: Complaint 659.

brick_1000.source: Fired-brick walls stand for generations when roofed and repaired; taken as most of a lifetime or more. Estimate.

stone_blocks.source: Dressed-stone walls outlast brick; Roman and medieval masonry buildings still stand. Estimate of the time to rebuild.

cement_portland_kg.source: Design working life of building structures, 50 years, in EN 1990 (Eurocode: Basis of structural design), table 2.1 category 4.

bronze_kg.source: Working life of a hand tool, blade or fitting before wear, breakage or loss replaces it; harder metals outlast softer, cutting edges wear fastest. Estimate.

merchant_ship.source: Rudan et al. 2024, Heritage 7, 6712-6728, doi:10.3390/heritage7120310, section 1, opened (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/f049/335ac58c23206e2cba18a0e74431f425ee8d.pdf): Kyrenia built in the second half of the fourth century BC and lost in the first decades of the third. Thirty years is an estimate within that archaeological interval, not a measured mean; old timber dates are not treated as the vessel age. Repairs are folded into replacement wear pending the carrier-capital maintenance model (complaint 629).

warship.source: D. H. Kennedy, Cable Reinforcement of the Athenian Trireme, Mariners Mirror 62 (1976), doi:10.1080/00253359.1976.10658957: about twenty years, mostly laid up. The publisher indexed extract was checked; full text was inaccessible. This is the reported approximate service life, not a guarantee under continuous service. Coates, Trireme Life Span and Leakage (2012), identifies leakage and deformation as physical limits; full chapter recalled, not reopened. Replacement wear includes refits until maintenance is separated (complaint 629).

ox.source: Langdon (Horses, Oxen and Technological Innovation, 1986) via Medievalists.net, https://www.medievalists.net/2023/02/horse-ox-medieval-times/ (the Medievalists.net page was opened in Complaint 646 pass 5; the book was not): 'plow horses and oxen typically have roughly the same life expectancy (a little over 5 years)' and 'the cart horse lives an average of around 7 years'. Five kept. A working life, not an age at death; the butchered animal's byproducts are the herd recipes' business, not carriage's.

mule.source: LABELLED HEURISTIC, no source found for a mule's working life (Complaint 646 pass 5: NCAT Draft Animal Power for Farming gives 'Approximately 15 years; ages 3-18' for draft horses only and nothing for mules; Langdon via Medievalists.net gives about 7 years for the cart horse, see ox); mules are taken as longer lived in work than horses and oxen; retire: Complaints/646.

cart.source: Research Project on Improved Food Crop Marketing Through Appropriate Transport for Poor Farmers in Uganda, 'The Economics of Intermediate Means of Transport', Final Report (R8114), assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/57a08c6440f0b652dd0012d6/R8114040502.pdf, Table 2 'IMT utilisation data': 'Average vehicle life (year) 10 20 20 15' for bicycle, pack donkey, donkey cart, oxen cart; 'Source: Consultant's estimate from transport operator's surveys'. Fifteen years is the oxen cart (fourth column). A modern Ugandan operator estimate with repairs folded in, not an archaeological figure (was 10, no source). Geography's CART_SERVICE_LIFE_KM is a different, unsourced heuristic.

pack_saddle.source: Estimate for a leather-and-wood pack rig in regular use, repairs folded in. Geography's PACK_SADDLE_SERVICE_LIFE_KM is an unsourced placeholder.

river_barge.source: Estimate, shorter than the seagoing merchant ship's 30 years (a river barge grounds and is hauled by rope); repairs folded in. Geography's BARGE_SERVICE_LIFE_KM is an unsourced placeholder.
